stem: Calculate the mean binding energy per nucleon for the formation of \(^{16}_{8}\mathrm{O}\) nucleus. The mass of oxygen atom is 15.994 u. The masses of H atom and neutron are 1.0078 u and 1.0087 u, respectively.
solution:
i. The mass defect, \(\Delta m = Z m_{\mathrm{H}} + (A - Z) m_{\mathrm{n}} - m\)

\(m_{\mathrm{H}} = 1.0078\ \mathrm{u}\), \(m_{\mathrm{n}} = 1.0087\ \mathrm{u}\) and \(m = 15.994\ \mathrm{u}\), \(Z = 8\), \(A = 16\)

\(\Delta m = 8 \times 1.0078\ \mathrm{u} + 8 \times 1.0087\ \mathrm{u} - 15.994\ \mathrm{u} = 0.137144\ \mathrm{u}\)

ii. Total binding energy, B.E. (MeV) \(= \Delta m\ (\mathrm{amu}) \times 931.4\)

Hence, B.E. \(= 0.137144 \times 931.4 = 127.73\ \mathrm{MeV}\)

iii. Binding energy per nucleon, \(\overline{B} = \dfrac{\mathrm{B.E.}}{A}\)

Hence, \(\overline{B} = \dfrac{127.73\ \mathrm{MeV}}{16} = 7.98\ \mathrm{MeV/nucleon}\)

The half life of \(^{32}\mathrm{P}\) is 14.26 d. What percentage of \(^{32}\mathrm{P}\) sample will remain after 40 d?
solution:
\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{14.26\ \mathrm{d}} = 0.0486\ \mathrm{d^{-1}}\)

Now, \(\lambda = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\ \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{N_0}{N}\right)\)

\(N_0 = 100\), \(N = ?\), \(t = 40\ \mathrm{d}\)

Hence, \(\log_{10}\dfrac{N_0}{N} = \dfrac{\lambda t}{2.303} = \dfrac{0.0486\ \mathrm{d^{-1}} \times 40\ \mathrm{d}}{2.303} = 0.8441\)

Taking antilog of both sides we get

\(\dfrac{N_0}{N} = \mathrm{antilog}\ (0.8441) = 6.984\)

\(\dfrac{100}{N} = 6.984\) or \(N = \dfrac{100}{6.984} = 14.32\)

% \(^{32}\mathrm{P}\) that remains after 40 d = 14.32 %

stem: The half life of \(^{34}\mathrm{Cl}\) is 1.53 s. How long does it take for 99.9 % of sample of \(^{34}\mathrm{Cl}\) to decay?
The half life of \(^{209}\mathrm{Po}\) is 102 y. How much of 1 mg sample of polonium decays in 62 y?
solution:
\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{102\ \mathrm{y}} = 6.794 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{y^{-1}}\)

\(\lambda = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\ \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{N_0}{N}\right)\)

Hence, \(\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{N_0}{N}\right) = \dfrac{\lambda t}{2.303}\)

or, \(\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{N_0}{N}\right) = \dfrac{6.794 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{y^{-1}} \times 62\ \mathrm{y}}{2.303} = 0.1829\)

It then follows that \(\dfrac{N_0}{N} = \mathrm{antilog}\ (0.1829) = 1.524\)

\(N = \dfrac{N_0}{1.524} = \dfrac{1\ \mathrm{mg}}{1.524} = 0.656\ \mathrm{mg}\)

N the amount that remains after 62 y. Hence, the amount decayed in 62 y \(= 1\ \mathrm{mg} - 0.656\ \mathrm{mg} = 0.344\ \mathrm{mg}\)

stem:
How many \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\)- particles are emitted in the following?

\(^{237}_{93}\mathrm{Np} \longrightarrow{} ^{209}_{83}\mathrm{Bi}\)
solution:
The emission of one \(\alpha\) - particle decreases the mass number by 4 whereas the emission of \(\beta\)- particles has no effect on mass number.

Net decrease in mass number \(= 237 - 209 = 28\). This decrease is only due to \(\alpha\)- particles.

Hence number of \(\alpha\)- particles emitted \(= \dfrac{28}{4} = 7\)

Now the emission of one \(\alpha\)-particle decreases the atomic number by 2 and \(\beta\)-particle emission increases by 1.

The net decrease in atomic number \(= 93 - 83 = 10\)

The emission of 7 \(\alpha\)-particles causes decrease in atomic number by 14. However the actual decrease is only 10. It means atomic number increses by 4. This increase is due to emission of \(\beta\)-particles. Thus, 4 \(\beta\)- particles are emitted.

stem:
Estimate the energy released in the fusion reaction

\(^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H} + {}^{3}_{2}\mathrm{He} \longrightarrow {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He} + {}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H}\)

Given atomic masses : \(^{2}\mathrm{H}\) = 2.041 u, \(^{3}\mathrm{He}\) = 3.0160 u, \(^{4}\mathrm{He}\) = 4.0026 u, \(^{1}\mathrm{H}\) = 1.0078 u
solution:
Mass defect \(\Delta m = (\text{mass of } ^{2}\mathrm{H} + \text{mass of } ^{3}\mathrm{He}) - (\text{mass of } ^{4}\mathrm{He} + \text{mass of } ^{1}\mathrm{H})\)

\(= 2.0141\ \mathrm{u} + 3.0160\ \mathrm{u} - 4.0026\ \mathrm{u} - 1.0078\ \mathrm{u} = 0.0197\ \mathrm{u}\)

\(E = \Delta m\ (\mathrm{u}) \times 931.4 = 0.0197\ \mathrm{u} \times 931.4 = 18.35\ \mathrm{MeV}\)

stem: Half life of \(^{209}\mathrm{Po}\) is 102 y. How many \(\alpha\)-particles are emitted in 1 s from 2 mg sample of Po?
solution:
Activity = number of \(\alpha\) (or \(\beta\)) particles emitted

\(= -\dfrac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N\)

\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{(102 \times 365 \times 24 \times 3600)\ \mathrm{s}} = 2.154 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\)

\(N = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-3} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}}{209} = 5.763 \times 10^{18}\) atoms of nuclei

\(-\dfrac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N = 2.154 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} \times 5.763 \times 10^{18}\ \text{atoms} = 1.241 \times 10^{9}\ \text{particles}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\)
